items.title: I tried to listen to music
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
Sometimes online, I stumble upon posts of people born before music streaming was a thing and they explain how listening to new music back then was an experience.

They would go to the shop, buy a CD or vinyl after struggling to choose. Then they'd come home, and listen to the music they had just bought. Nothing more, simply sitting there and listening.

This is really foreign to me as I've always seen music as a commodity. Music is the thing you put in the car, while washing the dishes, when you have a long walk to go somewhere, what's on at the radio when you're grocery shopping.

It is never about the music itself, more like an enjoyable background noise that you pay some attention to, but never all your attention.

And it makes sense that it works that way for me, because music has always been so easily available in nearly infinite quantities so it seems like a nice but unimportant thing.

items.title: Maps and Copyright
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt: A fascinating post on Worlds Revealed, the Library of Congress map blog, about some of the difficulties the Library faces when navigating map copyright. In particular, how global crises—World War II and the collapse of the Soviet Union are the examples explored—mess with who owns what maps, and complicate whether a given holding can be shared with the public. The U.S. seized the copyrights of German maps during World War II as an emergency expedient—only the German maps were in many cases captured Soviet maps. And when a federation collapses (the Soviet Union, Yugoslavia), state succession does not always make it clear which country holds the copyright on a given map.

items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
Inspiration for anti-surface warfare (ASuW) expeditionary strikepod operations can be found in coastal torpedo defense systems of World War II, as well as modern day coastal defense concepts.

During World War II, coastal torpedo batteries were constructed to defend ports, harbors, and coastal infrastructure against enemy shore bombardment or amphibious operations.

These installations were defensive in nature, employing either unguided torpedoes or wire-guided weapons controlled by operators ashore, with ranges varying by system.

The modern iteration, the expeditionary strikepod, would be capable of both offensive and defensive operations, contributing to both sea denial and sea control. Strikepod nodes (AUV/torpedoes) could operate autonomously at longer ranges, or conceivably with RF guidance.

I do not have an HSA. I would like to have one. I don't understand how I get from "I do not have an HSA" to "I have an HSA." My employer does not offer them. My health insurance plan is HSA eligible.

I have investments with a few companies but none of them offer plain ol' HSAs. At this point I just want to get one open and put in the minimum amount, so I can cross it off my to do list. If you have an HSA you're happy with and it isn't through your work, how did you get it?

items.title: Where do you keep your mail?
items.label: Q&A
items.excerpt:
That's it. That's the question. We get a fair amount of postal mail (a few bills that aren't paperless-available, lots of junk that gets recycled, some magazines, The London Review of Books, holiday cards, catalogs, etc.) There's...

This isn't about reducing the mail I get. It's about how to deal with what I keep. I flip through for recycling on the way back up from the mailbox, and usu ditch those things instantly. But I find the rest of it just...it's in piles all over. End of the kitchen table, things on the island and the coffee table, yes I have a basket and it gets full full full. How have YOU solved this? What are your mail habits?

items.title: Feed the Scorchpot [$14.99] [Strategy] [Windows] [macOS]
items.label: Gaming
items.excerpt:
You struck a deal with a dragon: twenty years of protection for twenty years of dinner service. The island thrives under the beast's watchful eye, as long as the meals keep coming.

Every year, the dragon wakes up hungrier. You roll dice to work your island, harvest ingredients, fuse them into recipes, and cook them down in the Scorchpot — the pot you keep full or end up in. Get the meal right and you prosper. Get it wrong and you're smoke.

Build farmsteads, shrines, and harbors across your hex-grid island, each one changing how the board pays out. The best runs start with a handful of tiles and end with a machine that buries the dragon in food. Then the odds tighten, the dragon turns picky, and you tear the whole thing down and rebuild while it's on fire.

Feed the Scorchpot, keep the dragon happy, and outlast the contract.

Cook cleverly, plan badly, or just roll with it — the dragon doesn't care how you win, only that you feed the beast on time. And yes, you can pet the…
